tells: NOSE: upgov[.]net, a domain urlscan lists as ten years old, with the page buried at /images/z1dpeth/-/louwhan1/pages/login.php. A login deep inside an images folder on an unrelated site doesn't belong there. Spotify signs people in at accounts[.]spotify[.]com.

PALATE: 'Welcome back', an email or username box, then Continue with phone number, Google, Facebook and Apple. The record shows the buttons, not where they lead. On a page like this, each one is a chance to collect a different sign-in.

FINISH: the page is in English but the reCAPTCHA notice at the bottom is in French, a mismatch copied pages often leave behind. urlscan rated it Potentially Malicious and detected Spotify. Open the app, or type the address yourself.
items.critic_note: An English 'Welcome back' over a French reCAPTCHA notice, poured from a domain that has spent ten years in the cellar with no connection to music. The login was found resting in an images folder, which is not where Spotify keeps its front door.

tells: Feature one: the address! att-103444-106506[.]square[.]site puts AT&T's name on a subdomain of Square's website builder, where anyone can claim a name. The registered part is square[.]site, not anything AT&T owns. Start at att[.]com instead.

But wait, there's more: 'Sign in to access AT&T Mail and Currently[.]com', a User ID box, a password box, and 'Powered by Square' at the bottom. Real email logins aren't built with a shop builder, and a borrowed reCAPTCHA notice doesn't change that.

Order now and get the record: urlscan rated it Potentially Malicious and detected AT&T. The footer still says © 2025 on a November 2026 scan. Never type an email password into a page you reached from a link; go to your provider yourself.
items.critic_note: Tired of signing in to your email provider? Now you can type your AT&T password into an online-store builder instead! Every kit ships with two strings of random numbers, a 2025 copyright and a 'Powered by Square' footer, because your inbox deserves the same platform as a cupcake shop. Operators are standing by. The operators are the scammers.

tells: Your reading: a GOV.UK header over energybillpayment[.]com. UK government services live on gov[.]uk addresses. A payment scheme hosted on a plain .com is the first card in the spread, and it isn't a good one.

A prediction: a '£100 Energy Payment for eligible households', paid from January 2027, but only if you register. The eligibility list includes 'a valid bank account for payment'. Check any scheme on gov[.]uk yourself before giving anyone your details.

The outlook: urlscan rated it Potentially Malicious and detected UK Government; the submitter tagged it a threat. The capture stops at 'What you need to register', so the form itself isn't in the record. Don't give bank details to a sign-up page you reached by link.
items.critic_note: The stars foresee £100 arriving in January 2027, a forecast delivered from a .com dressed in a GOV.UK header. Charts this generous always want something first. This one wants you to register, and it has already mentioned your bank account.

tells: Note the address: a run of letters, then twenty digits, then meusitehostgator[.]com[.]br, the domain of a website-builder service where customers get their own subdomains. Netflix signs people in at netflix[.]com, not on a builder's shelf.

Observe the form: 'Entrar', with boxes for 'Email ou número de celular' and 'Senha', copied right down to the reCAPTCHA notice. A good copy is the whole point, so how the page looks proves nothing. Only the address can.

Consider the record: urlscan rated it Potentially Malicious and detected Netflix. The page also prints a phone number under 'Dúvidas?'. A number on a copied page may be copied or swapped, so look it up on the real site before you call.
items.critic_note: A faithful study of the Netflix sign-in, rendered in Portuguese on a website-builder subdomain that runs to twenty digits. The red is correct and the brushwork is confident. The frame, however, was assembled by a hosting company's site tool, and Netflix did not commission it.

tells: AFFECTED PRODUCT: 'Payment Verification — USPS' at uspsfund[.]online, a domain urlscan saw on the day it was registered. USPS is at usps[.]com. A .online address with 'fund' bolted on is somebody else's mailbox.

HAZARD: a 'held parcel', a $1.95 redelivery fee, then a form for cardholder name, card number, expiry, CVV, billing address, phone and email, 'for fraud prevention purposes'. The tiny fee is the hook; the card details are the catch.

REMEDY: urlscan rated it Potentially Malicious and detected USPS. Don't pay delivery fees through a link in a text or email. Type the tracking number into usps[.]com yourself. The '256-bit SSL' badge only means the connection to the thief is private.
items.critic_note: Effective immediately, this redelivery portal is withdrawn from service. A $1.95 fee was found to require a card number, expiry date, CVV, billing address, phone number and email address. The paperwork outweighs the postage by a margin we could not justify.

tells: Clue one: the address, hastana[.]org/auth/google/index.html. A folder named google on someone else's domain is just a folder. Google sign-in happens on accounts[.]google[.]com.
Clue two: the cover story, 'Sign in with Google to continue to hastanaindonesia[.]id'. It borrows the familiar 'continue to' line from real third-party sign-ins, which is why the swap feels routine.

Clue three: suspected phishing, not confirmed. urlscan gave no classification; community tags mark it as possible Google phishing, on a domain seen the day it was registered. Real Google sign-in moves the address bar to Google.
items.critic_note: The sign-in box looked exactly like Google's. That was the problem. Google serves its own sign-in pages, and this one was coming out of a folder called /auth/google/ on hastana[.]org.

tells: VIOLATION #1: afirmennet[.]info borrows the name of Afirme's online banking, AfirmeNet, adds an n and moves it to .info. Afirme's own site is afirme[.]com.
VIOLATION #2: a copied homepage with an AfirmeNet entry point and a car-insurance offer of 'hasta 30% de descuento'. A faithful front door is how a lookalike earns the click on its login link.
VIOLATION #3: suspected phishing, not confirmed. urlscan gave no classification, though community tags flag it as a phishing threat. Log in from the bank's app or a typed address.
items.critic_note: Inspection found a full Afirme homepage, insurance discount and all, operating from afirmennet[.]info, a domain urlscan saw on the day it was registered. The extra n was not on the permit.

tells: The address is phantomactivate[.]com, about three weeks old when scanned. Phantom's own site is phantom[.]com, and wallets don't have a separate 'activate' website.
It opens on create.php under 'Add a Wallet', promising seamless setup and easy recovery. Setup pages on lookalike domains are where visitors get asked to import an existing recovery phrase.

urlscan rated it Potentially Malicious and detected Phantom Wallet; the submitter tagged it seed-phrase harvesting. The capture shows the first screen only. Never type a recovery phrase into a website.
items.critic_note: I never asked to activate anything, and the page still wanted to add a wallet for me. Phantom doesn't need activating, and it doesn't live at phantomactivate[.]com. One star, and 'Easy recovery' is doing a lot of work.

items.page_title: Pagos por Cuenta Contrato de la EAAB ESP
tells: The setup: Bogotá's water company takes payments at acueducto[.]com[.]co. This page reshuffles those words into acueducto-co-com[.]st, a different domain under a different country ending.
The play: 'Pagos por Cuenta Contrato', a lookup by account number with a debt type and a spreadsheet upload for paying several accounts. A bill lookup is a natural lead-in to asking for card details.

The review: urlscan rated it Potentially Malicious with a Colombian government brand match, and the community tagged it for takedown. The capture stops before payment. Pay utility bills from the official site or your bank.
items.critic_note: Tidy little move: take the utility's real address, acueducto[.]com[.]co, shuffle the pieces into acueducto-co-com, and finish on .st. The bill form even asks visitors to prove they're human, which is bold coming from this side of the field.

tells: It nests at bt-internet-mail-106245[.]weeblysite[.]com. weeblysite[.]com belongs to the Weebly site builder, and the name in front is whatever the sign-up typed. BT Email lives on bt[.]com.
It displays one plain sign-in, 'Email address or username' and 'Password', with a reCAPTCHA notice for an official feel. A webmail login on a website builder is a credential form in costume.
urlscan rated it Potentially Malicious and detected BT. The capture shows the form, not a submission. Reach BT Email by typing bt[.]com or using the app.
items.critic_note: Here, on a free website builder, a creature calling itself BT Internet Mail has nested at subdomain number 106245. It has mastered exactly two fields, email and password, and left the builder's 'eCommerce by Square' badge lying behind it.

items.page_title: Ocean Bank | The Power of Ocean
tells: Red flag: read the address from the right. qzz[.]io is the registered domain; 'lorealparis' and 'oceanicredit' are labels its owner stacked on top. Neither the bank nor the cosmetics company is in charge here.
Red flag: it copies a current holiday notice, closed Thursday, November 26, and was scanned within hours of it. Timely details make a fake feel maintained. Check the address, not the news banner.
Red flag: urlscan rated it Potentially Malicious and detected Ocean Bank, and the capture shows a Username and Password box. Bank only at the address printed on your card or statement. Swipe left.
items.critic_note: Says he's a bank: FDIC-insured, closed for Thanksgiving, very proud of his financial results. Lives at oceanicredit[.]lorealparis[.]qzz[.]io, which is a bank inside a cosmetics brand inside qzz[.]io. Great with holidays, bad with commitment.

tells: It comes with the address teiswpop[.]top, so new that urlscan saw it the day it was registered. Telegram's web app runs at web[.]telegram[.]org.

But wait, there's more: one screen, one field, 'Please confirm your country code and enter your phone number.' Account-takeover pages take the number, then the login code Telegram sends you. Never type that code into a page.
urlscan rated it Potentially Malicious and detected Telegram. The scan captures the phone step only. Log in from the app or web[.]telegram[.]org, and turn on two-step verification.
items.critic_note: Operators are standing by to take your phone number! This Telegram Web comes with a blue paper plane, a country picker preset to the United States and a domain, teiswpop[.]top, that sounds like a sneeze.

VIOLATION #3: urlscan rated it Potentially Malicious and detected Coinbase. The scan also shows Yandex Metrica tracking loading. Open exchanges by typing their address, not from 'official site' lookalikes.

items.page_title: Trezor Wallet App (Official) | Desktop & Web Crypto Management
tells: AFFECTED PRODUCT: a Trezor Wallet storefront, scanned from trezor-suite[.]im and landing on trez-apps-web[.]com, which urlscan saw on the day it was registered. Neither is trezor[.]io.

items.critic_note: Recalled for arriving through a checkpoint. Visitors to trezor-suite[.]im were sent to checking.php with a 32-character ticket before the shop opened on trez-apps-web[.]com, a third address that also isn't Trezor's.

tells: Exhibit A: trezozxolgein[.]gitbook[.]io. GitBook hosts documents for anyone; the string in front is a mash of trezor and login. Trezor's own site is trezor[.]io.
Exhibit B: the title 'Trezor® - Login | US | - Log_in' and a notice that a Trezor Suite update is ready to install. Updates arrive inside the Suite app, never through a hosted doc page.
Exhibit C: urlscan rated it Potentially Malicious and detected Trezor. The scan was bounced to /us, and the page links out once; where that link goes isn't shown. Get Suite only from trezor[.]io.

items.page_title: Set Up Your Ledger Device | Ledger.com/start Official Guide
tells: The browser tab says 'Set Up Your Ledger Device | Ledger[.]com/start' while the page says 'Get started with your new Trezor'. Two brands, one page. A real setup guide knows which company made it.

But wait, there's more: portal-start-docs-trezr-io[.]typedream[.]app. 'trezr-io' is spelled out as decoration on a free site builder, and the footer says Made in Typedream. Trezor's setup lives at trezor[.]io/start.

urlscan rated it Potentially Malicious and detected Trezor. The page pushes 'Download Trezor Suite' and 'Continue in browser'; what those deliver isn't in the record. Install wallet software only from the maker.
items.critic_note: Call now and get a Trezor setup guide, a Ledger tab title and a free 'Made in Typedream' badge! That's two wallet brands for the price of zero domains of your own.

tells: The address is trezorcloud[.]io and the page is entirely D'CENT. One wallet maker's name in the address and another's logo on the page means neither company built it.

Its 'Get started' button leads into getstarted.php, and the submitter tagged the page seed-phrase harvesting. A setup flow for a hardware wallet that lives on someone else's domain is exactly where recovery phrases get typed.

Suspected phishing, not confirmed: urlscan gave this visit no classification, and the capture stops before any phrase is requested. The rule holds anyway: a hardware wallet never needs its recovery phrase typed into a website.
items.critic_note: Ordered a D'CENT wallet. The box said trezorcloud. The page said D'CENT. The only thing the two brands agree on is that neither of them lives here. One star, and I'm keeping my recovery phrase.

tells: With ogin rising before murfin-drilling[.]com, someone wanted 'login' and kept everything but the l. The registered domain is murfin-drilling[.]com, and a Microsoft security check has no reason to live there.
Mercury is in 'Widget error. Please refresh the page.' twice. A broken verification box is still a stage set: it trains you to keep refreshing and to trust whatever screen comes next.
urlscan rated it Potentially Malicious and detected Microsoft. The capture stops at the check, so the sign-in it guards isn't recorded. Your lucky address today is one you type yourself.
items.critic_note: The stars see a login page that lost its first letter on the way to the subdomain, parked on a domain named for drilling. Today's reading: a security check that cannot check its own widget.

tells: VIOLATION #1: Adobe branding served from pattwhitney[.]com, a domain urlscan dates to about 1,255 days old with no Adobe in its name. Document Cloud lives on adobe[.]com.

VIOLATION #2: a pre-filled 'YOUR VERIFICATION CODE' with a Copy Code button and an instruction to continue and paste it. Real codes arrive by text or email and you type them yourself. A page that asks you to copy and paste deserves suspicion.

VIOLATION #3: suspected phishing, not confirmed. urlscan gave no classification; the submitter tagged it phishing. The capture doesn't show what was copied or where 'Continue to Adobe' leads. Open files from Adobe's own site.
items.critic_note: Inspection found a document portal that hands each customer a verification code and then asks the customer to paste it back. The establishment does not appear to be Adobe. The sign on the door says pattwhitney[.]com.

tells: Clue one: the address. msn-lime[.]vercel[.]app is a project on Vercel's hosting, not a Microsoft domain. The scan even began at www[.]msn-lime and was bounced to the bare name.

Clue three: urlscan rated it Potentially Malicious and detected Microsoft; the tab title is just 'Iniciar'. The next screen isn't in this capture. Sign in only through microsoft[.]com or the app.
items.critic_note: Microsoft was updating its terms, the page said. Microsoft does say that a lot, which is exactly why it works. The question nobody asked was why the announcement came from msn-lime[.]vercel[.]app.

tells: The hostname opens with two long runs of digits and ends in workers[.]dev, Cloudflare's hosting for scripts that anyone can deploy to. Apple signs people in at icloud[.]com, not on a rented subdomain.

urlscan rated it Potentially Malicious and detected Apple. The footer still says Copyright © 2024 Apple Inc. on a fresh scan. If iCloud asks you to verify something, go to icloud[.]com yourself.
items.critic_note: A minimalist piece: an iCloud logo, a security check, a 'Nie jestem robotem' box and a 2024 copyright on a page scanned in November 2026. The address is longer than the page.

items.page_title: Axelar | The Gateway To Cross-Chain Rewards
tells: Note the spelling: app.axeiar-vote[.]xyz has an i where Axelar has an l. At small sizes the two letters are nearly identical, which is the entire technique. Compare addresses with a bookmark, letter by letter.
Observe the offer: 'Participate in the Axelar community vote and receive a 1.25x multiplier on your reward claims.' A vote that pays a bonus is bait. Governance doesn't need a stranger's link.

Consider the record: suspected phishing, not confirmed. urlscan gave this visit no classification, while the submitter tagged it a crypto drainer. The screenshot shows the pitch, not what 'connect' would sign. Treat any wallet prompt here as hostile.
items.critic_note: Acquired from an anonymous donor, this piece is labelled Axelar, but the plaque on the address reads axeiar. Note the 1.25x reward multiplier offered to every visitor who votes, a feature the art world calls a provenance problem.

tells: The setup: a cloned header with Personas, Tienda en línea and Paquetes y Recargas, served from ytelcelyou[.]art. A 'y' glued to an .art domain isn't telcel[.]com, however tidy the menu looks.

The play: '¡Tienes puntos disponibles para canjear!' followed by 'No dejes que tus puntos caduquen.' Rewards that are about to expire are a clock, and clocks rush you past the address bar. Check points in the official app.

The replay booth: urlscan rated it Potentially Malicious and detected Telcel. The capture stops at 'Consulta tus puntos', so what that button collects isn't in the record. Don't give a points page your number or card.
items.critic_note: He fakes left with Telcel's real menu, spins past the sustainability blurb, and shoots for your phone number with a points balance nobody asked about. Then the replay shows the arena: ytelcelyou[.]art. Even the stadium is offside.

tells: NOSE: details-xaman[.]app, which urlscan saw on the day it was registered. Xaman's own site is xaman[.]app; a word bolted on the front makes a different domain with a different owner.

PALATE: one headline, one paragraph, one 'Claim Airdrop' button. Real airdrops are announced inside the wallet and on official channels. A claim page you reach by link is the classic way to get a wallet to sign away its assets.

FINISH: urlscan rated it Potentially Malicious with a generic crypto match; the submitter tagged it a drainer. The scan shows the button, not what it would ask you to sign. Never connect a wallet to claim something you didn't expect.
items.critic_note: Complimentary XRP, poured by a domain whose only contribution is the word 'details'. The page announces the airdrop is activated, then offers exactly one thing to do about it.

Red flag: the 'Recent activity' feed is a column of truncated wallets voting YES or NO minutes apart. The scan proves the page displays that feed, not where it comes from. A crowd on a page is decoration until you can check it elsewhere.

Red flag: urlscan rated it Potentially Malicious and detected Moonshot; the submitter tagged it a drainer. Voting with a wallet means signing something. Only vote or connect from the real app. Swipe left.
